aspectTitle: Border/boundary contrast bites ONLY when it is the sole cue that a control exists
aspectDescription: The SC's UI-component requirement only applies to the visual information NECESSARY to identify that a control is present. The Understanding text is explicit: a border indicating the hit area is required to contrast 3:1 only 'when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control'; if the control has visible text or a sufficiently contrasting icon, a low-contrast surrounding border is NOT subject to the requirement. So the identical low-contrast 2px grey border can be a PASS on a labelled, clearly-styled button and a FAIL on a borderless 'ghost' input whose ONLY cue is that s
scenario: Civic permit-search page with two side-by-side search inputs sharing the identical 2px #AAAAAA border (2.32:1): the left has a visible 'Search by address' label + placeholder (PASS, border exempt); the right 'case number' box is bare with no label/placeholder/icon (FAIL, border is the only cue and required).
mechanism: The case-number input's only visual cue that a control exists is a 2.32:1 grey border, below the 3:1 threshold; because no other visual way identifies the control, the boundary is required and fails. The identical border on the labelled address input is exempt because its visible label identifies the control.

aspectTitle: State-indicator (checked/selected/expanded) contrast against the CORRECT adjacent surface within the component
aspectDescription: Beyond identifying that a control exists, the SC requires the non-text information that conveys STATE -- the check in a checkbox, the dot in a radio, the thumb of a toggle/slider, the chevron showing an accordion is open -- to have 3:1 against ITS adjacent color, which may be another part of the component rather than the page. Two semantic judgements are needed that automation cannot make: (a) identifying which mark conveys state versus which is decorative, and (b) choosing the correct comparison surface (the check is measured against the box fill, not the page; the toggle thumb against the tr
scenario: Healthcare patient-portal consent form with custom checkboxes. Two boxes are CHECKED: the box fills brand-purple #6221EA and contrasts ~7:1 with the white card (distractor PASS), but the check mark is a brand tint #9D85DB drawn on that fill at 2.33:1 — the checked-state mark fails its correct adjacent surface (the box fill).
mechanism: The checked-state indicator (SVG check stroke #9D85DB) sits on the purple fill #6221EA at 2.33:1, below the 3:1 required for non-text information that indicates state. The correct adjacent color for an internal state mark is the box fill, not the page; box-vs-page (7.18:1) is a distractor.

Group B (deductible) uses mark-on-fill: a faint inner dot #7BB0E6 on a #4A90D9 fill at 1.46:1 (FAIL). Same blue palette, opposite verdicts depending on the correct adjacent surface.

scenario: Restaurant review star ratings, the 1.4.1-vs-1.4.11 boundary. Each rating is also text ('4 of 5'), so Use of Color is satisfied (not hue-only). Default reviews still FAIL 1.4.11: a 'filled' star is distinguished from empty only by an inner glow #C99A3E on the gold body #A67C2E at 1.47:1. The value-as-text removes the 1.4.1 concern, isolating the 1.4.11 mark-vs-body failure. The solid-fill variant (17:1) marks the conforming boundary.

aspectTitle: Selecting WHICH parts of a complex graphic are 'required for understanding' and whether equivalent text exempts them
aspectDescription: G207/G209 require 3:1 contrast only for graphical objects 'required for understanding.' The whole judgement is meaning-level: in a multi-part graphic (chart line, pie slice, infographic circle + its icon, map region, the magnet's U-shape and tips) the evaluator must decide WHICH parts a viewer must perceive to grasp the meaning, then test only those -- and crucially the graphic is EXEMPT if equivalent text (visible labels AND values, or a data table via a Long Description) conveys the same information. So a pie chart with adjoining 1.5:1 slices is a FAIL when the slices are the only data, NOT
scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard renders a 'Browser market share Q2 2026' pie chart as inline SVG with four adjoining pastel wedges (~1.1-1.3:1 between neighbours) and NO labels, values, legend, or data table. The slice boundaries are the only data and are the graphical objects required for understanding.
mechanism: Adjoining pie wedges (#6FA8DC / #93C47D / #E0A0A0 / #E8C8E0) differ by only ~1.1-1.3:1 with no 3:1 separating border; per G209 the slice boundaries are graphical objects required for understanding and must reach 3:1 (or carry a 3:1 border). With no labels+values to exempt them, the chart fails.

scenario: A college advancement report shows 'Where our alumni connect' as a bubble infographic in inline SVG: five circles whose AREA encodes community size, each with a faint inner icon marking the platform. Circle-vs-page (~1.26:1) and icon-vs-circle (~1.30:1) are both below 3:1, with no member counts/legend/table; the text names give identity but not size.

aspectTitle: F78: an author focus indicator that technically exists but is rendered non-visible by surrounding styling
aspectDescription: F78 names failure modes beyond the trivial outline:none: (a) a non-focus outline/border that looks identical to the browser focus ring, so the user cannot tell which element is focused; and (b) a thick element border the same color as the focus indicator drawn just outside it, so the focus ring is swallowed by the border. In both cases an outline IS present on focus -- a CSS scraper or rule that merely detects a focus style reports a pass -- but a sighted keyboard user cannot perceive WHICH control has focus or that focus moved at all. Deciding this requires comparing the focused appearance ag
scenario: Glyphwright SDK API-reference 'On this page' link rail: every TOC link permanently carries a 1px dotted #1b1b1b outline, and :focus re-declares the identical 1px dotted #1b1b1b outline at the same offset. Page loads (autofocus) with the Pagination link focused; it is visually indistinguishable from its eight siblings.
mechanism: F78(a): the author's always-on decorative outline is byte-identical to the focus indicator (same 1px/dotted/#1b1b1b/offset), so the focused link's appearance equals the resting appearance of every other link — focus state carries zero discriminating signal even though a focus outline genuinely renders. Verified in Chrome: the focused Pagination link looks exactly like the other links.

mechanism: F78(b): the focus outline is the same color (black) as a thicker (4px) element border drawn immediately inside it, so the focus ring is swallowed — it reads as one continuous black edge with only a hairline gap. Verified in Chrome close-up: the focused button differs from the unfocused one by an imperceptible thin black line, not a discernible focus change. (An explicit black author outline is used rather than the UA default, which modern Chrome paints in the accent color and would not be occluded.)

aspectTitle: F78: an author focus indicator that technically exists but is rendered non-visible by surrounding styling
aspectDescription: F78 names failure modes beyond the trivial outline:none: (a) a non-focus outline/border that looks identical to the browser focus ring, so the user cannot tell which element is focused; and (b) a thick element border the same color as the focus indicator drawn just outside it, so the focus ring is swallowed by the border. In both cases an outline IS present on focus -- a CSS scraper or rule that merely detects a focus style reports a pass -- but a sighted keyboard user cannot perceive WHICH control has focus or that focus moved at all. Deciding this requires comparing the focused appearance ag
scenario: Hearthline real-estate listing card grid (PASS boundary): every card has a subtle resting box-shadow, but :focus-visible swaps to a thick high-contrast offset ring — outline:3px solid #1b3a2b, outline-offset:4px, plus a wide 6px colored halo. Page loads (autofocus) with the 8 Meadowgate Ct card focused.
mechanism: Correct F78 avoidance: the focus indicator differs from the resting decoration on multiple axes at once (solid vs soft, dark-green vs translucent grey, 4px offset vs flush, plus wide halo), so the focused card is unmistakably distinct and the ~9:1 ring exceeds the 3:1 focus-state threshold. Verified in Chrome: the focused card is clearly identifiable among its neighbours. Included so the judge must reason about discernibility, not mere presence of a focus style.

aspectTitle: Choosing the correct comparison surface: subsumed borders/shadows and controls between two backgrounds
aspectDescription: The 'Adjacent colors' guidance requires the evaluator to pick the meaningful comparison and ignore decorative elements. A border between two contrasting backgrounds, or a 3D drop-shadow, is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness' and is NOT measured; instead you measure inside vs outside background. A background-color-only input (no border) is measured against the page (#043464 example). Getting the verdict right means deciding which color is the meaningful adjacent one and which decorative element to ignore -- e.g. an input on a dark panel whose silver border is irrelevant because the
scenario: Online-banking wire form. Text inputs with a white interior and a thin graphite border (#3E5168) sit on a dark-blue panel (#003366). A per-edge tool measures border-vs-panel = 1.55:1 and reports a 1.4.11 failure; the correct verdict is PASS because the graphite border is subsumed into the dark panel and the meaningful adjacency is the white interior vs the dark-blue panel (12.6:1).
mechanism: Subsumption rule: a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness', so it is not measured; the identifying cue is the white interior vs the #003366 panel at 12.6:1. The border (1.55:1 vs panel) does not interfere with identifying the control and is ignored.

aspectTitle: Focus-indicator geometry: which adjacency the indicator must contrast with (inner / on-the-border / partly-outside)
aspectDescription: Where a focus indicator sits determines which adjacency it must contrast with, and the SC carves out specific patterns that automation cannot disambiguate. An indicator entirely OUTSIDE need only contrast with the page the component sits on. An indicator entirely INSIDE must contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component. An indicator that IS the component's border must contrast with BOTH adjacencies. A partly-inside/partly-outside indicator passes if EITHER part contrasts. So an inner green border that contrasts with the black outer border but NOT with the blue component background
scenario: Meridian online-banking transfer-confirm screen. Two brand-blue (#4189B9) primary buttons with a 2px black border, side by side. On focus each draws a 3px INSET ring inside the visible boundary: #btn-confirm uses dark-green #008000 (FAIL), #btn-schedule uses white (PASS). The only difference is the ring colour; the verdict flips on which INNER adjacency the indicator must beat.
mechanism: An inner focus indicator (box-shadow inset) must contrast with the adjacent colour WITHIN the component. The green inset ring contrasts the black border (4.09:1) but, being entirely inside the blue button, must beat the blue interior (#4189B9) — green-on-blue is 1.35:1, far below 3:1, so the focused state is imperceptible to a moderately-low-vision user. The white-ring sibling beats the blue interior at 3.82:1 and passes.

The focus indicator is a 4px yellow (#FFFF00) ring that STRADDLES each seat's boundary — a 2px inset half (inside the seat) plus a 2px outset half (outside on the cabin page), via two stacked box-shadows. aspectTitle: Negative/NA boundaries: inactive controls, hover-only treatments, essential graphics & author-choice logos, and symbolic text characters
aspectDescription: The SC defines several carve-outs whose correct answer is 'Not Applicable / Pass' and which a naive contrast scan will wrongly FAIL, plus one inclusion (symbolic text) it will wrongly ignore. (1) Inactive/disabled controls are exempt -- a faint disabled button is NOT a failure. (2) Author-supplied HOVER treatments are supplemental and need not contrast 3:1 because the pointer position is the indicator. (3) The Essential exception exempts logos/flags/sensory photos/heatmaps/medical schematics -- BUT a logo presented low-contrast by AUTHOR CHOICE (not brand-mandated, e.g. dark-grey logos on a bl
scenario: Auto-insurance checkout: an operable 'Pay now' submit button and a natively-disabled 'Enroll in AutoPay' button share pixel-identical 'ghost' styling — a 2px #c9c9c9 border (~1.66:1 on white). The active button FAILS (its identifying border is the only thing marking the control and must reach 3:1); the disabled twin is exempt (inactive UI).
mechanism: An active UI component's identifying boundary (2px #c9c9c9 border ≈1.66:1 vs white) is below the 3:1 non-text-contrast threshold; the inactive-UI exemption applies only to the disabled twin, not to the operable #pay-now submit, so the surface fails.
